solution: Substitute $x=\tan\theta$ to get $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan\theta)\,d\theta$. Since $1+\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta+\cos\theta}{\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\sqrt2\,\cos(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\theta)}{\cos\theta}$, we have $\ln(1+\tan\theta)=\tfrac12\ln2+\ln\cos(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\theta)-\ln\cos\theta$. Integrating from $0$ to $\pi/4$ and using $\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln\cos(\tfrac{\pi}{4}-\theta)\,d\theta=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\ln\cos u\,du$, the logarithm terms cancel, leaving $I=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}\tfrac12\ln2\,d\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{8}\ln2$.
